summary:
Consensual same-sex sexual activity is lawful in Peru under the 1924 Penal Code; the 1863 code had criminalised sodomy with penalties comparable to those for rape. The age of consent is 14 irrespective of gender or sexual orientation, following a 2012 Constitutional Court decision, and applies to trans and cisgender youth alike. Trans identity is not itself an offence.

No legal protection against discrimination or hate crime on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity is in force. Government Decree Nº 1323 criminalised such discrimination with effect from 7 January 2017 through Articles 46 and 323 of the Penal Code. Congress voted 66 to 29 in May 2017 to strip those provisions, after an April Constitutional Committee vote and a petition for removal carrying one million signatures; the repeal was carried by Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members, who argued that the president had lacked authority to issue the decree.

Public facilities are now the sharpest documented restriction. The April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents mandates that entry to public restrooms be determined by "biological sex", which bars trans people, including trans youth, from facilities matching their gender identity. Bills 6505/2023-CR and 8457/2023-CR, presented by legislators including Jorge Montoya and members of Honor y Democracia, ban restroom use contrary to birth sex and prohibit inclusive signage such as "women in their diversity"; on 20 February 2025 a congressional committee approved the dictamen of bills 6506 and 8457 unanimously for plenary. Law 32331, enacted 13 May 2025, is recorded as prohibiting trans people from using public restrooms, a state-imposed limit on daily movement in transit spaces.

The IDEHPUCP human-rights institute of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru assesses the restriction as open discrimination against trans and non-binary people, since it bars access to facilities matching gender identity and implicitly frames trans people as harassment risks. The institute cites Inter-American Court of Human Rights Advisory Opinion OC-24/17, under which gender identity falls within protected personal autonomy and states must guarantee trans people full rights, and quotes congressman Lizarzaburu's dehumanising comparisons of trans people.

The same April 2025 law carries censorship provisions. Article 4 bans media and advertising content on vague grounds and Article 5 enables suppression of identity, artistic and educational material, while the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years. Human Rights Watch states that child protection is used as a pretext for repression and for the scapegoating of trans people.

State violence against a trans person has produced a documented conviction. On 15 December 2025 police officers Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It is Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per the reporting, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history, reaching the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

A report of 22 July 2024 found recorded hate crimes rising in Peru with trans women most affected. Its co-author, trans human-rights defender and journalist Gianna Camacho, states that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry of what occurred.

Healthcare provision has moved in both directions within a single year. In May 2024 the government decreed "transsexualism" a mental health problem in order to cover trans healthcare; after protests, in June 2024 the Ministry of Health revised the term to "gender discordance" for health-insurance classification purposes, and health authorities removed pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients. In May 2024 the Ministry of Health also reiterated that sexual orientation and gender identity are not diseases.

Legal documents: transgender Peruvians may change their legal name to match their gender identity. The Constitutional Court barred gender-marker changes on national identity documents in 2014, then reversed itself in a ruling of 21 October 2016 published on 8 November 2016, permitting gender change through a judicial process without sex-reassignment surgery. A Gender Identity Law covering legal gender change without surgery and access to passports and other identity documents matching gender identity was introduced on 4 November 2016 and remained pending in the legislature as of March 2021.

Protection machinery is contested rather than absent. Public institutions themselves contribute to anti-LGBTIQ discrimination. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, acting on an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional. The April 2025 NGO foreign-funding law allows authorities to revoke registrations on public order and security grounds, which risks being used against queer organising.
tangentialFactors:
After the May 2017 repeal of the anti-discrimination provisions, Peru is described as one of only three South American countries, alongside Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in its penal framework. The comparison is a count of jurisdictions, not a measure of comparative risk.

Hostility has been voiced against elected officials. Willax TV presenter Ana María Salcedo publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to "go use the men's room"; the incident is recorded in an April 2025 account of setbacks to gender, LGBTIQ and reproductive rights.

Community demands recorded alongside the February 2025 committee vote include supply of HIV medication, scrapping of outdated medical rules, recognition of diverse families, equal marriage, and LGBTIQ+ quotas in public office. Congressional pressure against therapeutic abortion at the Instituto Nacional Materno Perinatal continues in the same period.

Pride marches have been held annually in Peru since 2002, with the oldest recorded march dated 1984.

Public opinion data in this inventory is dated and measures attitudes to gay and lesbian people rather than to trans people: 18 to 24-year-olds were markedly more favourable toward homosexuals at 66 per cent against 49 per cent overall, and same-sex marriage approval stood at 8.3 per cent among Peruvians in 2010, higher among younger respondents. These figures describe historical opinion, not current conditions for trans visitors.
localsOnly:
Legal gender recognition runs through the courts. Following the Constitutional Court's reversal of its 2014 position, a judicial process permits change of gender marker on national identity documents without sex-reassignment surgery, and legal name change to match gender identity is available. The Gender Identity Law introduced on 4 November 2016, which would place legal gender change without surgery and matching passports and identity documents on a statutory footing, remained pending in the legislature as of March 2021; its status after that date is not sourced here.

Conversion therapy is banned in Peru for medical professionals, and in May 2024 the Ministry of Health reiterated that sexual orientation and gender identity are not diseases, a protection with specific relevance to trans and LGBTQ minors exposed to such practices. The June 2024 revision of the health-insurance classification from "transsexualism" to "gender discordance" and the removal of pathologising terminology from official health guidance govern how trans patients are treated in the health system.

The 2016 national education curriculum includes information on sexual orientation, sex and gender issues, describing sexual orientation as the result of complex biological, cognitive and environmental circumstances and "not a voluntary choice".

A 2012 study by the Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia found that 70 per cent of trans women in Lima and Callao work in sex work. The figure is a 2012 measurement of residents of those two cities and is not a current national estimate.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory conflicts on the outcome of the May 2017 vote. One source records that Congress stripped the provisions and that the repeal took effect, while another records that the president's veto stood. This is unresolved here. Both readings agree that no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity is currently in force.

The relationship between the legislative instruments restricting restroom use is unresolved. Sources describe bills 6505/2023-CR and 6506/2023-CR together with bill 8457/2023-CR at committee stage in February 2025, an April 2025 sexual-integrity law containing a biological-sex restroom rule, and Law 32331 enacted 13 May 2025 recorded as prohibiting trans people from using public restrooms. Whether these are one package or several, and which is currently operative, is not established by the sources.

No enforcement data exists in this inventory for the restroom restriction: no documented inspections, penalties, prosecutions or challenged incidents of its application are recorded, and no border or airport screening procedure specific to trans travellers is documented.

The July 2024 hate-crime report gives no counts, no denominator and no measurement period, and its co-author states the figures are a sub-registry. The magnitude of trans-directed hate crime relative to general crime rates in Peru therefore cannot be assessed from these sources.

The "anti-equality decree" struck down by the Lima constitutional court in July 2025 is not identified by number or content in the inventory, and the court's reasoning is not sourced.

Whether the Gender Identity Law introduced in November 2016 has advanced, been enacted or been withdrawn after March 2021 is not sourced.
